```text
src/
├── app/
├── components/
│   └── nested-tabs/
│       ├── nested-tabs.tsx
│       ├── nested-tabs.test.tsx
│       └── nested-tabs.stories.tsx
├── features/
├── hooks/
├── services/
├── store/
├── pages/
├── routes/
├── utils/
├── constants/
├── types/
├── styles/
└── tests/
```

### Project Architecture
Use feature-based boundaries so the component can evolve without creating a large shared-components dependency graph.

### Component Breakdown
- `Nestedtabs` container
- Presentational primitives
- State/interaction hook
- Async/data boundary if required
- Empty/loading/error components

### State Management Design
Keep ephemeral UI state local. Use Zustand/Redux Toolkit only when state is shared across independent consumers. Use TanStack Query for server state instead of duplicating request lifecycle state in global stores.

### API Layer Design
Expose typed service functions, centralize request behavior, normalize errors, support cancellation and keep credentials/security policy out of UI components.

### Custom Hooks
Suggested hook: `useNestedTabs`. The hook should expose behavior, not DOM implementation details.

### Utilities
- Keep pure transformations in utilities.
- Unit test utilities independently.
- Avoid utilities that hide stateful behavior.

### Type Definitions
```ts
export type ComponentItem = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
};

export type ComponentProps = {
  items: readonly ComponentItem[];
  onChange?: (item: ComponentItem) => void;
};
```

### Constants
```ts
export const UI_LIMITS = {
  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Error Handling Strategy
Use typed application errors at the service boundary, local recoverable UI states for expected failures, and Error Boundaries for unexpected render failures.

### Loading Strategy
Prefer skeletons for stable layouts, spinners for short blocking operations, and Suspense/lazy loading for route or component boundaries.

### Empty State
Explain what is empty, why it is empty when known, and provide the most useful next action.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useState } from "react";

type Props = { items: string[] };

export function Component({ items }: Props) {
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string | null>(null);

  return (
    <section aria-label="Interactive component">
      {items.map((item) => (
        <button
          key={item}
          type="button"
          aria-pressed={selected === item}
          onClick={() => setSelected(item)}
        >
          {item}
        </button>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

### Bad Implementation → Good Implementation
❌ **Bad:** put every state value in a global store, fetch directly from presentational components, duplicate interaction logic, omit keyboard support, and render thousands of nodes without virtualization.  
↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

### Expected Behavior
The **Nested tabs** component should remain predictable under normal use, repeated interactions, loading/error conditions and responsive layouts.

### Data Flow
```text
User Event
   ↓
Handler
   ↓
State / Mutation
   ↓
Derived State
   ↓
Render
   ↓
Browser Paint
```

```text
Idle
 ├──→ Loading ──→ Success
 │                  └──→ Empty
 └──→ Error ──→ Retry
```

```text

   ↓
Custom Hook
   ↓
Query / Mutation Layer
   ↓
API Client
   ↓
Backend
```

### Performance Diagram
```text
Input
 ↓
Debounce / Batch
 ↓
Minimal State Update
 ↓
Selective Render
 ↓
Commit
 ↓
Paint
```

### Testing Strategy
- **Vitest:** pure utilities and hooks.
- **React Testing Library:** user-visible component behavior.
- **Playwright:** critical end-to-end flows.
- **Storybook:** isolated component states.
- **Accessibility:** keyboard and accessible-name assertions.

### Storybook Integration
```tsx
export const Default = {
  args: {
    items: [
      { id: "1", label: "First" },
      { id: "2", label: "Second" },
    ],
  },
};
```

### Deployment Considerations
- Production build with Vite.
- Environment-specific API configuration.
- Bundle analysis.
- Source-map policy appropriate to security requirements.
- CI checks for type errors, lint, unit tests and E2E smoke tests.

### Production Notes
Add observability for failures and latency, avoid logging sensitive data, verify responsive behavior, test slow networks and ensure accessibility regressions are caught before deployment.

- [ ] Semantic HTML
- [ ] Keyboard complete
- [ ] Focus visible
- [ ] Accessible names
- [ ] Error messages associated with controls
- [ ] Dynamic updates announced where required

### Performance Audit
- [ ] React DevTools Profiler reviewed
- [ ] No unnecessary global state
- [ ] Large collections virtualized
- [ ] Network requests debounced/cancelled where needed
- [ ] Lazy loading applied to appropriate boundaries
- [ ] Bundle impact measured

### Security Review
- [ ] Untrusted HTML is never rendered without a deliberate sanitization policy
- [ ] External URLs are validated
- [ ] Sensitive data is not placed in logs
- [ ] API authorization is enforced server-side
- [ ] Third-party dependencies are reviewed

### Interview Follow-up Questions
1. How would you make this component reusable across products?
2. How would you test keyboard and screen-reader behavior?
3. What happens with 100,000 records?
4. How would you handle slow or failed APIs?
5. Which state belongs locally versus globally?
6. Where would you use memoization, and how would you prove it helps?
7. How would you evolve the API without breaking consumers?
8. How would you instrument this in production?

### Time Complexity
For a typical list interaction, rendering is **O(n)** in the number of rendered items. With virtualization, the DOM work becomes approximately **O(v)** where `v` is the visible window, while data operations may remain O(n) depending on the algorithm.

### Space Complexity
Typical component state is **O(1)** or **O(n)** depending on whether selection/order/cache state is retained per item. Virtualization reduces DOM memory, not necessarily application data memory.

### Scalability Discussion
At Staff/Principal level, discuss component contracts, design-system governance, shared ownership, performance budgets, observability, versioning, accessibility compliance and migration strategy.

### Debugging Walkthrough
1. Reproduce the issue.
2. Inspect component props/state in React DevTools.
3. Profile renders with React Profiler.
4. Inspect network requests.
5. Check browser console and accessibility tree.
6. Add a focused regression test.
7. Re-measure after the fix.

- [ ] Requirements are explicit
- [ ] Component API is minimal
- [ ] State ownership is justified
- [ ] Async race conditions handled
- [ ] Accessibility verified
- [ ] Responsive behavior verified
- [ ] Performance measured
- [ ] Tests cover behavior
- [ ] Storybook states exist
- [ ] Error/loading/empty states exist

- Prefer simple local state before introducing global state.
- Build reusable APIs, not reusable complexity.

### Time Complexity

Typical component state is **O(1)** or **O(n)** depending on whether selection/order/cache state is retained per item. Virtualization reduces DOM memory, not necessarily application data memory.

- State must remain consistent after repeated interactions.
- Edge cases must not crash the application.

### Performance Requirements
- Avoid unnecessary rendering.
- Debounce/throttle high-frequency events where appropriate.
- Virtualize large lists/grids.
- Lazy-load expensive features.

### Responsive Requirements
Design mobile-first behavior, define layout breakpoints, preserve usable touch targets, and ensure content remains accessible at narrow widths.

### Problem Analysis

### API Layer Design

### Custom Hooks

### Utilities

### Type Definitions
```ts

  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
};

export type ComponentProps = {

};
```

### Constants

```ts
  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Error Handling Strategy
Use typed application errors at the service boundary, local recoverable UI states for expected failures, and Error Boundaries for unexpected render failures.

### Loading Strategy
Prefer skeletons for stable layouts, spinners for short blocking operations, and Suspense/lazy loading for route or component boundaries.

### Empty State
Explain what is empty, why it is empty when known, and provide the most useful next action.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useState } from "react";

export function ExampleForm() {
  const [name, setName] = useState("");

  function submit(event: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
    event.preventDefault();
    if (!name.trim()) return;
    console.log({ name });
  }

  return (
    <form onSubmit={submit} noValidate>
      <label htmlFor="name">Name</label>
      <input
        id="name"
        name="name"
        value={name}
        onChange={(e) => setName(e.target.value)}
        required
      />
      <button type="submit">Save</button>
    </form>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

```tsx
}
```

- Focus must be managed for overlays and composite widgets.
- ARIA must supplement—not replace—semantic HTML.

### Performance Requirements
- Avoid unnecessary rendering.
- Debounce/throttle high-frequency events where appropriate.
- Virtualize large lists/grids.
- Lazy-load expensive features.

### Responsive Requirements
Design mobile-first behavior, define layout breakpoints, preserve usable touch targets, and ensure content remains accessible at narrow widths.

### Problem Analysis
Identify the primary interaction model for **Tabs Storybook**, then split it into presentational components, stateful logic, reusable hooks, data services and test boundaries.

### Low-Level Design
- Props define the public contract.
- Hooks own reusable behavior.
- Components render derived state.
- Services isolate API/network concerns.
- Utilities contain deterministic pure functions.

### High-Level Design
```text
Page
 ↓
Feature Container
 ├── UI Components
 ├── Custom Hooks
 ├── Query / API Layer
 ├── Client State
 └── Tests / Storybook
```

### Folder Structure
```text
src/
├── app/
├── components/
│   └── tabs-storybook/
│       ├── tabs-storybook.tsx
│       ├── tabs-storybook.test.tsx

├── routes/
├── utils/
├── constants/

├── styles/
└── tests/
```

### Project Architecture
Use feature-based boundaries so the component can evolve without creating a large shared-components dependency graph.

### Component Breakdown
- `TabsStorybook` container
- Presentational primitives
- State/interaction hook
- Async/data boundary if required
- Empty/loading/error components

### State Management Design
Keep ephemeral UI state local. Use Zustand/Redux Toolkit only when state is shared across independent consumers. Use TanStack Query for server state instead of duplicating request lifecycle state in global stores.

### API Layer Design
Expose typed service functions, centralize request behavior, normalize errors, support cancellation and keep credentials/security policy out of UI components.

### Custom Hooks
Suggested hook: `useTabsStorybook`. The hook should expose behavior, not DOM implementation details.

### Utilities
- Keep pure transformations in utilities.
- Unit test utilities independently.
- Avoid utilities that hide stateful behavior.

### Type Definitions
```ts
export type ComponentItem = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
};

export type ComponentProps = {
  items: readonly ComponentItem[];
  onChange?: (item: ComponentItem) => void;
};
```

### Constants
```ts

  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Error Handling Strategy
Use typed application errors at the service boundary, local recoverable UI states for expected failures, and Error Boundaries for unexpected render failures.

### Loading Strategy
Prefer skeletons for stable layouts, spinners for short blocking operations, and Suspense/lazy loading for route or component boundaries.

### Empty State
Explain what is empty, why it is empty when known, and provide the most useful next action.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useState } from "react";

type Props = { items: string[] };

export function Component({ items }: Props) {
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string | null>(null);

  return (
    <section aria-label="Interactive component">
      {items.map((item) => (
        <button
          key={item}
          type="button"
          aria-pressed={selected === item}
          onClick={() => setSelected(item)}
        >
          {item}
        </button>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

❌ **Bad:** put every state value in a global store, fetch directly from presentational components, duplicate interaction logic, omit keyboard support, and render thousands of nodes without virtualization.  
↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

```text
 ↓
```

### Performance Audit

- [ ] Lazy loading applied to appropriate boundaries

- [ ] External URLs are validated
- [ ] Sensitive data is not placed in logs

1. How would you make this component reusable across products?
2. How would you test keyboard and screen-reader behavior?
3. What happens with 100,000 records?
4. How would you handle slow or failed APIs?
5. Which state belongs locally versus globally?
6. Where would you use memoization, and how would you prove it helps?
7. How would you evolve the API without breaking consumers?
8. How would you instrument this in production?

### Time Complexity
For a typical list interaction, rendering is **O(n)** in the number of rendered items. With virtualization, the DOM work becomes approximately **O(v)** where `v` is the visible window, while data operations may remain O(n) depending on the algorithm.

### Space Complexity
Typical component state is **O(1)** or **O(n)** depending on whether selection/order/cache state is retained per item. Virtualization reduces DOM memory, not necessarily application data memory.

4. Inspect network requests.
5. Check browser console and accessibility tree.
6. Add a focused regression test.
7. Re-measure after the fix.

- [ ] Error/loading/empty states exist

```tsx
import { useState } from "react";

type Props = { items: string[] };

export function Component({ items }: Props) {
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string | null>(null);

  return (
    <section aria-label="Interactive component">
      {items.map((item) => (
        <button
          key={item}
          type="button"
          aria-pressed={selected === item}
          onClick={() => setSelected(item)}
        >
          {item}
        </button>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx

  label: string;
};

  items,
  onSelect,

  items: readonly Item[];

}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

```tsx
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

type DialogProps = {
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
};

export function Dialog({ open, onClose }: DialogProps) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (open) ref.current?.showModal();
    else if (ref.current?.open) ref.current.close();
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <dialog ref={ref} onCancel={onClose} aria-labelledby="dialog-title">
      <h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm action</h2>
      <button type="button" onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
    </dialog>
  );
}
```

## Question 62 — Accessible dialog

**Module:** Module 4 – Modal & Dialog  
**Difficulty:** ⭐ Easy  
**Expected Time:** 20 Minutes  
**Experience Level:** 2–5 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Problem Statement
Build a production-quality **Accessible dialog** component suitable for a machine-coding interview. The implementation must be reusable, accessible, responsive, typed, testable and explainable.

### Business Requirements
- Provide the core **Accessible dialog** behavior.
- Support normal, loading, empty and error states where applicable.
- Keep the public component API small and predictable.

### Functional Requirements
- User interactions must update UI state correctly.
- State must remain consistent after repeated interactions.
- Edge cases must not crash the application.
- Async work must handle cancellation/race conditions where applicable.

### Non-functional Requirements
- React 19+ and TypeScript
- Clean feature-based architecture
- Reusable components and hooks
- Responsive and accessible UI
- Testable behavior

### UI Requirements
- Use semantic HTML.
- Provide visible interaction states.
- Support mobile and desktop layouts.
- Provide loading, empty and error feedback when relevant.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Keyboard navigation must work.
- Interactive elements must have accessible names.
- Focus must be managed for overlays and composite widgets.
- ARIA must supplement—not replace—semantic HTML.

### Performance Requirements
- Avoid unnecessary rendering.
- Debounce/throttle high-frequency events where appropriate.
- Virtualize large lists/grids.
- Lazy-load expensive features.

### Responsive Requirements
Design mobile-first behavior, define layout breakpoints, preserve usable touch targets, and ensure content remains accessible at narrow widths.

### Problem Analysis
Identify the primary interaction model for **Accessible dialog**, then split it into presentational components, stateful logic, reusable hooks, data services and test boundaries.

### Low-Level Design
- Props define the public contract.
- Hooks own reusable behavior.
- Components render derived state.
- Services isolate API/network concerns.
- Utilities contain deterministic pure functions.

### High-Level Design
```text
Page
 ↓
Feature Container
 ├── UI Components
 ├── Custom Hooks
 ├── Query / API Layer
 ├── Client State
 └── Tests / Storybook
```

### Folder Structure
```text
src/
├── app/
├── components/
│   └── accessible-dialog/
│       ├── accessible-dialog.tsx
│       ├── accessible-dialog.test.tsx
│       └── accessible-dialog.stories.tsx
├── features/
├── hooks/
├── services/
├── store/
├── pages/
├── routes/
├── utils/
├── constants/
├── types/
├── styles/
└── tests/
```

### Project Architecture
Use feature-based boundaries so the component can evolve without creating a large shared-components dependency graph.

### Component Breakdown
- `Accessibledialog` container
- Presentational primitives
- State/interaction hook
- Async/data boundary if required
- Empty/loading/error components

### State Management Design
Keep ephemeral UI state local. Use Zustand/Redux Toolkit only when state is shared across independent consumers. Use TanStack Query for server state instead of duplicating request lifecycle state in global stores.

### API Layer Design
Expose typed service functions, centralize request behavior, normalize errors, support cancellation and keep credentials/security policy out of UI components.

### Custom Hooks
Suggested hook: `useAccessibleDialog`. The hook should expose behavior, not DOM implementation details.

### Utilities
- Keep pure transformations in utilities.
- Unit test utilities independently.
- Avoid utilities that hide stateful behavior.

### Type Definitions
```ts
export type ComponentItem = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
};

export type ComponentProps = {
  items: readonly ComponentItem[];
  onChange?: (item: ComponentItem) => void;
};
```

### Constants
```ts
export const UI_LIMITS = {
  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Error Handling Strategy
Use typed application errors at the service boundary, local recoverable UI states for expected failures, and Error Boundaries for unexpected render failures.

### Loading Strategy
Prefer skeletons for stable layouts, spinners for short blocking operations, and Suspense/lazy loading for route or component boundaries.

### Empty State
Explain what is empty, why it is empty when known, and provide the most useful next action.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

type DialogProps = {
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
};

export function Dialog({ open, onClose }: DialogProps) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (open) ref.current?.showModal();
    else if (ref.current?.open) ref.current.close();
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <dialog ref={ref} onCancel={onClose} aria-labelledby="dialog-title">
      <h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm action</h2>
      <button type="button" onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
    </dialog>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

### Bad Implementation → Good Implementation
❌ **Bad:** put every state value in a global store, fetch directly from presentational components, duplicate interaction logic, omit keyboard support, and render thousands of nodes without virtualization.  
↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

### Expected Behavior
The **Accessible dialog** component should remain predictable under normal use, repeated interactions, loading/error conditions and responsive layouts.

### Data Flow
```text
User Event
   ↓
Handler
   ↓
State / Mutation
   ↓
Derived State
   ↓
Render
   ↓
Browser Paint
```

### State Diagram
```text
Idle
 ├──→ Loading ──→ Success
 │                  └──→ Empty
 └──→ Error ──→ Retry
```

### API Diagram
```text
Component
   ↓
Custom Hook
   ↓
Query / Mutation Layer
   ↓
API Client
   ↓
Backend
```

### Performance Diagram
```text
Input
 ↓
Debounce / Batch
 ↓
Minimal State Update
 ↓
Selective Render
 ↓
Commit
 ↓
Paint
```

### Testing Strategy
- **Vitest:** pure utilities and hooks.
- **React Testing Library:** user-visible component behavior.
- **Playwright:** critical end-to-end flows.
- **Storybook:** isolated component states.
- **Accessibility:** keyboard and accessible-name assertions.

### Storybook Integration
```tsx
export const Default = {
  args: {
    items: [
      { id: "1", label: "First" },
      { id: "2", label: "Second" },
    ],
  },
};
```

### Deployment Considerations
- Production build with Vite.
- Environment-specific API configuration.
- Bundle analysis.
- Source-map policy appropriate to security requirements.
- CI checks for type errors, lint, unit tests and E2E smoke tests.

### Production Notes
Add observability for failures and latency, avoid logging sensitive data, verify responsive behavior, test slow networks and ensure accessibility regressions are caught before deployment.

### Accessibility Audit
- [ ] Semantic HTML
- [ ] Keyboard complete
- [ ] Focus visible
- [ ] Accessible names
- [ ] Error messages associated with controls
- [ ] Dynamic updates announced where required

### Performance Audit
- [ ] React DevTools Profiler reviewed
- [ ] No unnecessary global state
- [ ] Large collections virtualized
- [ ] Network requests debounced/cancelled where needed
- [ ] Lazy loading applied to appropriate boundaries
- [ ] Bundle impact measured

### Security Review
- [ ] Untrusted HTML is never rendered without a deliberate sanitization policy
- [ ] External URLs are validated
- [ ] Sensitive data is not placed in logs
- [ ] API authorization is enforced server-side
- [ ] Third-party dependencies are reviewed

### Interview Follow-up Questions
1. How would you make this component reusable across products?
2. How would you test keyboard and screen-reader behavior?
3. What happens with 100,000 records?
4. How would you handle slow or failed APIs?
5. Which state belongs locally versus globally?
6. Where would you use memoization, and how would you prove it helps?
7. How would you evolve the API without breaking consumers?
8. How would you instrument this in production?

### Time Complexity
For a typical list interaction, rendering is **O(n)** in the number of rendered items. With virtualization, the DOM work becomes approximately **O(v)** where `v` is the visible window, while data operations may remain O(n) depending on the algorithm.

### Space Complexity
Typical component state is **O(1)** or **O(n)** depending on whether selection/order/cache state is retained per item. Virtualization reduces DOM memory, not necessarily application data memory.

### Scalability Discussion
At Staff/Principal level, discuss component contracts, design-system governance, shared ownership, performance budgets, observability, versioning, accessibility compliance and migration strategy.

### Debugging Walkthrough
1. Reproduce the issue.
2. Inspect component props/state in React DevTools.
3. Profile renders with React Profiler.
4. Inspect network requests.
5. Check browser console and accessibility tree.
6. Add a focused regression test.
7. Re-measure after the fix.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] Requirements are explicit
- [ ] Component API is minimal
- [ ] State ownership is justified
- [ ] Async race conditions handled
- [ ] Accessibility verified
- [ ] Responsive behavior verified
- [ ] Performance measured
- [ ] Tests cover behavior
- [ ] Storybook states exist
- [ ] Error/loading/empty states exist

### Mini Project
Build a complete **Accessible dialog** feature with mock API support, loading/error/empty states, responsive design, accessibility audit, Storybook stories, Vitest tests and Playwright coverage.

### Production Exercise
Take the initial **Accessible dialog** implementation and evolve it for enterprise scale: add server integration, caching, error recovery, telemetry, feature flags and performance instrumentation.

### Assignment
Implement **Accessible dialog** in 45–60 minutes, then spend 15 minutes explaining architecture, trade-offs, accessibility, performance and testing decisions.

### Revision Notes
- Analyze → design → implement core path → handle states → accessibility → performance → testing → explain trade-offs.
- Prefer simple local state before introducing global state.
- Build reusable APIs, not reusable complexity.

### Cheat Sheet
**Requirements → LLD → HLD → Components → State → Hooks → API → Edge Cases → Accessibility → Performance → Tests → Storybook → Production.**

```tsx
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

type DialogProps = {
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
};

export function Dialog({ open, onClose }: DialogProps) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (open) ref.current?.showModal();
    else if (ref.current?.open) ref.current.close();
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <dialog ref={ref} onCancel={onClose} aria-labelledby="dialog-title">
      <h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm action</h2>
      <button type="button" onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
    </dialog>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

### Bad Implementation → Good Implementation
❌ **Bad:** put every state value in a global store, fetch directly from presentational components, duplicate interaction logic, omit keyboard support, and render thousands of nodes without virtualization.  
↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

```ts
  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
};

};
```

```ts
  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useState } from "react";

type Props = { items: string[] };

export function Component({ items }: Props) {
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string | null>(null);

  return (
    <section aria-label="Interactive component">
      {items.map((item) => (
        <button
          key={item}
          type="button"
          aria-pressed={selected === item}
          onClick={() => setSelected(item)}
        >
          {item}
        </button>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

### Time Complexity
For a typical list interaction, rendering is **O(n)** in the number of rendered items. With virtualization, the DOM work becomes approximately **O(v)** where `v` is the visible window, while data operations may remain O(n) depending on the algorithm.

### Space Complexity
Typical component state is **O(1)** or **O(n)** depending on whether selection/order/cache state is retained per item. Virtualization reduces DOM memory, not necessarily application data memory.

### Constants
```ts
export const UI_LIMITS = {
  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Error Handling Strategy
Use typed application errors at the service boundary, local recoverable UI states for expected failures, and Error Boundaries for unexpected render failures.

### Loading Strategy
Prefer skeletons for stable layouts, spinners for short blocking operations, and Suspense/lazy loading for route or component boundaries.

### Empty State
Explain what is empty, why it is empty when known, and provide the most useful next action.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

type DialogProps = {
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
};

export function Dialog({ open, onClose }: DialogProps) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (open) ref.current?.showModal();
    else if (ref.current?.open) ref.current.close();
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <dialog ref={ref} onCancel={onClose} aria-labelledby="dialog-title">
      <h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm action</h2>
      <button type="button" onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
    </dialog>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

### Bad Implementation → Good Implementation
❌ **Bad:** put every state value in a global store, fetch directly from presentational components, duplicate interaction logic, omit keyboard support, and render thousands of nodes without virtualization.  
↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

### Expected Behavior
The **Nested dialogs** component should remain predictable under normal use, repeated interactions, loading/error conditions and responsive layouts.

```text
Render

```


```text
 ↓

 ↓

 ↓

 ↓
```

### Time Complexity
For a typical list interaction, rendering is **O(n)** in the number of rendered items. With virtualization, the DOM work becomes approximately **O(v)** where `v` is the visible window, while data operations may remain O(n) depending on the algorithm.

4. How would you handle slow or failed APIs?
5. Which state belongs locally versus globally?
6. Where would you use memoization, and how would you prove it helps?
7. How would you evolve the API without breaking consumers?
8. How would you instrument this in production?

### Time Complexity
For a typical list interaction, rendering is **O(n)** in the number of rendered items. With virtualization, the DOM work becomes approximately **O(v)** where `v` is the visible window, while data operations may remain O(n) depending on the algorithm.

### Space Complexity
Typical component state is **O(1)** or **O(n)** depending on whether selection/order/cache state is retained per item. Virtualization reduces DOM memory, not necessarily application data memory.

3. Profile renders with React Profiler.
4. Inspect network requests.
5. Check browser console and accessibility tree.
6. Add a focused regression test.
7. Re-measure after the fix.

- Edge cases must not crash the application.

- Clean feature-based architecture
- Reusable components and hooks
- Responsive and accessible UI
- Testable behavior

### UI Requirements
- Use semantic HTML.
- Provide visible interaction states.

- Provide loading, empty and error feedback when relevant.

### Accessibility Requirements

- Interactive elements must have accessible names.
- Focus must be managed for overlays and composite widgets.
- ARIA must supplement—not replace—semantic HTML.

### Performance Requirements
- Avoid unnecessary rendering.
- Debounce/throttle high-frequency events where appropriate.
- Virtualize large lists/grids.
- Lazy-load expensive features.

### Responsive Requirements
Design mobile-first behavior, define layout breakpoints, preserve usable touch targets, and ensure content remains accessible at narrow widths.

### Problem Analysis
Identify the primary interaction model for **Form dialog**, then split it into presentational components, stateful logic, reusable hooks, data services and test boundaries.

### Low-Level Design
- Props define the public contract.
- Hooks own reusable behavior.
- Components render derived state.
- Services isolate API/network concerns.

```text
Page
 ↓

 ├── Query / API Layer
```

```text
src/

└── tests/
```

### Component Breakdown
- `Formdialog` container
- Presentational primitives
- State/interaction hook
- Async/data boundary if required
- Empty/loading/error components

### State Management Design
Keep ephemeral UI state local. Use Zustand/Redux Toolkit only when state is shared across independent consumers. Use TanStack Query for server state instead of duplicating request lifecycle state in global stores.

### API Layer Design
Expose typed service functions, centralize request behavior, normalize errors, support cancellation and keep credentials/security policy out of UI components.

### Custom Hooks
Suggested hook: `useFormDialog`. The hook should expose behavior, not DOM implementation details.

### Utilities
- Keep pure transformations in utilities.
- Unit test utilities independently.
- Avoid utilities that hide stateful behavior.

### Type Definitions
```ts
export type ComponentItem = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
};

export type ComponentProps = {
  items: readonly ComponentItem[];
  onChange?: (item: ComponentItem) => void;
};
```

### Constants
```ts
export const UI_LIMITS = {
  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Error Handling Strategy
Use typed application errors at the service boundary, local recoverable UI states for expected failures, and Error Boundaries for unexpected render failures.

### Loading Strategy
Prefer skeletons for stable layouts, spinners for short blocking operations, and Suspense/lazy loading for route or component boundaries.

### Empty State
Explain what is empty, why it is empty when known, and provide the most useful next action.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

type DialogProps = {
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
};

export function Dialog({ open, onClose }: DialogProps) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (open) ref.current?.showModal();
    else if (ref.current?.open) ref.current.close();
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <dialog ref={ref} onCancel={onClose} aria-labelledby="dialog-title">
      <h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm action</h2>
      <button type="button" onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
    </dialog>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

### Bad Implementation → Good Implementation
❌ **Bad:** put every state value in a global store, fetch directly from presentational components, duplicate interaction logic, omit keyboard support, and render thousands of nodes without virtualization.  
↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

### Expected Behavior

```text
├── store/
├── pages/
├── routes/
├── utils/
├── constants/
├── types/
├── styles/
└── tests/
```

### Project Architecture
Use feature-based boundaries so the component can evolve without creating a large shared-components dependency graph.

### Component Breakdown
- `Loadingdialog` container
- Presentational primitives
- State/interaction hook
- Async/data boundary if required
- Empty/loading/error components

### State Management Design
Keep ephemeral UI state local. Use Zustand/Redux Toolkit only when state is shared across independent consumers. Use TanStack Query for server state instead of duplicating request lifecycle state in global stores.

### API Layer Design
Expose typed service functions, centralize request behavior, normalize errors, support cancellation and keep credentials/security policy out of UI components.

### Custom Hooks
Suggested hook: `useLoadingDialog`. The hook should expose behavior, not DOM implementation details.

### Utilities
- Keep pure transformations in utilities.
- Unit test utilities independently.
- Avoid utilities that hide stateful behavior.

### Type Definitions
```ts
export type ComponentItem = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
};

export type ComponentProps = {
  items: readonly ComponentItem[];
  onChange?: (item: ComponentItem) => void;
};
```

### Constants
```ts
export const UI_LIMITS = {
  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Error Handling Strategy
Use typed application errors at the service boundary, local recoverable UI states for expected failures, and Error Boundaries for unexpected render failures.

### Loading Strategy
Prefer skeletons for stable layouts, spinners for short blocking operations, and Suspense/lazy loading for route or component boundaries.

### Empty State
Explain what is empty, why it is empty when known, and provide the most useful next action.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

type DialogProps = {
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
};

export function Dialog({ open, onClose }: DialogProps) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (open) ref.current?.showModal();
    else if (ref.current?.open) ref.current.close();
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <dialog ref={ref} onCancel={onClose} aria-labelledby="dialog-title">
      <h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm action</h2>
      <button type="button" onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
    </dialog>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

### Bad Implementation → Good Implementation
❌ **Bad:** put every state value in a global store, fetch directly from presentational components, duplicate interaction logic, omit keyboard support, and render thousands of nodes without virtualization.  
↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

### Expected Behavior
The **Loading dialog** component should remain predictable under normal use, repeated interactions, loading/error conditions and responsive layouts.

```text
   ↓
Handler

State / Mutation
   ↓
Derived State
   ↓
Render
   ↓
Browser Paint
```

```text
 ├──→ Loading ──→ Success

```

```text
Custom Hook
   ↓
Query / Mutation Layer
   ↓

   ↓
Backend
```

```text
 ↓

 ↓
Minimal State Update
 ↓
Selective Render
 ↓
Commit
 ↓
Paint
```

- **React Testing Library:** user-visible component behavior.
- **Playwright:** critical end-to-end flows.
- **Storybook:** isolated component states.
- **Accessibility:** keyboard and accessible-name assertions.

```tsx
  args: {
    items: [
      { id: "1", label: "First" },
      { id: "2", label: "Second" },

};
```

2. How would you test keyboard and screen-reader behavior?
3. What happens with 100,000 records?
4. How would you handle slow or failed APIs?
5. Which state belongs locally versus globally?
6. Where would you use memoization, and how would you prove it helps?

### Time Complexity
For a typical list interaction, rendering is **O(n)** in the number of rendered items. With virtualization, the DOM work becomes approximately **O(v)** where `v` is the visible window, while data operations may remain O(n) depending on the algorithm.

### Space Complexity
Typical component state is **O(1)** or **O(n)** depending on whether selection/order/cache state is retained per item. Virtualization reduces DOM memory, not necessarily application data memory.

7. Re-measure after the fix.

## Question 77 — Dialog performance

**Difficulty:** ⭐ Easy  
**Expected Time:** 20 Minutes

### Problem Statement

### Business Requirements
- Provide the core **Dialog performance** behavior.
- Support normal, loading, empty and error states where applicable.
- Keep the public component API small and predictable.

### Functional Requirements
- User interactions must update UI state correctly.
- State must remain consistent after repeated interactions.
- Edge cases must not crash the application.
- Async work must handle cancellation/race conditions where applicable.

### Non-functional Requirements
- React 19+ and TypeScript
- Clean feature-based architecture
- Reusable components and hooks
- Responsive and accessible UI
- Testable behavior

### UI Requirements
- Use semantic HTML.
- Provide visible interaction states.
- Support mobile and desktop layouts.
- Provide loading, empty and error feedback when relevant.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Keyboard navigation must work.
- Interactive elements must have accessible names.
- Focus must be managed for overlays and composite widgets.
- ARIA must supplement—not replace—semantic HTML.

### Performance Requirements
- Avoid unnecessary rendering.
- Debounce/throttle high-frequency events where appropriate.
- Virtualize large lists/grids.
- Lazy-load expensive features.

### Responsive Requirements
Design mobile-first behavior, define layout breakpoints, preserve usable touch targets, and ensure content remains accessible at narrow widths.

### Problem Analysis
Identify the primary interaction model for **Dialog performance**, then split it into presentational components, stateful logic, reusable hooks, data services and test boundaries.

### Low-Level Design
- Props define the public contract.
- Hooks own reusable behavior.
- Components render derived state.
- Services isolate API/network concerns.
- Utilities contain deterministic pure functions.

```text
Page
 ↓

 ├── UI Components
 ├── Custom Hooks
 ├── Query / API Layer
 ├── Client State
 └── Tests / Storybook
```

### Component Breakdown

- Presentational primitives
- State/interaction hook
- Async/data boundary if required
- Empty/loading/error components

### State Management Design
Keep ephemeral UI state local. Use Zustand/Redux Toolkit only when state is shared across independent consumers. Use TanStack Query for server state instead of duplicating request lifecycle state in global stores.

### API Layer Design
Expose typed service functions, centralize request behavior, normalize errors, support cancellation and keep credentials/security policy out of UI components.

### Custom Hooks
Suggested hook: `useDialogPerformance`. The hook should expose behavior, not DOM implementation details.

### Utilities
- Keep pure transformations in utilities.
- Unit test utilities independently.
- Avoid utilities that hide stateful behavior.

### Type Definitions
```ts
export type ComponentItem = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
};

export type ComponentProps = {
  items: readonly ComponentItem[];
  onChange?: (item: ComponentItem) => void;
};
```

### Constants
```ts
export const UI_LIMITS = {
  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Error Handling Strategy
Use typed application errors at the service boundary, local recoverable UI states for expected failures, and Error Boundaries for unexpected render failures.

### Loading Strategy
Prefer skeletons for stable layouts, spinners for short blocking operations, and Suspense/lazy loading for route or component boundaries.

### Empty State
Explain what is empty, why it is empty when known, and provide the most useful next action.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

type DialogProps = {
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
};

export function Dialog({ open, onClose }: DialogProps) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (open) ref.current?.showModal();
    else if (ref.current?.open) ref.current.close();
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <dialog ref={ref} onCancel={onClose} aria-labelledby="dialog-title">
      <h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm action</h2>
      <button type="button" onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
    </dialog>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

### Bad Implementation → Good Implementation
❌ **Bad:** put every state value in a global store, fetch directly from presentational components, duplicate interaction logic, omit keyboard support, and render thousands of nodes without virtualization.  
↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

### Expected Behavior
The **Dialog performance** component should remain predictable under normal use, repeated interactions, loading/error conditions and responsive layouts.

- Virtualize large lists/grids.
- Lazy-load expensive features.

### Responsive Requirements

### Problem Analysis
Identify the primary interaction model for **Dialog Storybook**, then split it into presentational components, stateful logic, reusable hooks, data services and test boundaries.

### Low-Level Design
- Props define the public contract.
- Hooks own reusable behavior.
- Components render derived state.
- Services isolate API/network concerns.

Keep ephemeral UI state local. Use Zustand/Redux Toolkit only when state is shared across independent consumers. Use TanStack Query for server state instead of duplicating request lifecycle state in global stores.

Expose typed service functions, centralize request behavior, normalize errors, support cancellation and keep credentials/security policy out of UI components.

- Keep pure transformations in utilities.

Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

- Duplicate items

- Failed requests

- Small viewport

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useEffect, useRef } from "react";

type DialogProps = {
  open: boolean;
  onClose: () => void;
};

export function Dialog({ open, onClose }: DialogProps) {
  const ref = useRef<HTMLDialogElement>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    if (open) ref.current?.showModal();
    else if (ref.current?.open) ref.current.close();
  }, [open]);

  return (
    <dialog ref={ref} onCancel={onClose} aria-labelledby="dialog-title">
      <h2 id="dialog-title">Confirm action</h2>
      <button type="button" onClick={onClose}>Close</button>
    </dialog>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

### Time Complexity
For a typical list interaction, rendering is **O(n)** in the number of rendered items. With virtualization, the DOM work becomes approximately **O(v)** where `v` is the visible window, while data operations may remain O(n) depending on the algorithm.

### Space Complexity
Typical component state is **O(1)** or **O(n)** depending on whether selection/order/cache state is retained per item. Virtualization reduces DOM memory, not necessarily application data memory.

```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

export function SearchBox() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!query.trim()) return;
    const id = window.setTimeout(() => {
      console.log("search:", query);
    }, 300);
    return () => window.clearTimeout(id);
  }, [query]);

  return (
    <label>
      Search
      <input
        value={query}
        onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)}
        aria-label="Search"
      />
    </label>
  );
}
```

## Question 82 — Debounced search

**Module:** Module 5 – Autocomplete & Search  
**Difficulty:** ⭐ Easy  
**Expected Time:** 20 Minutes  
**Experience Level:** 2–5 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Problem Statement
Build a production-quality **Debounced search** component suitable for a machine-coding interview. The implementation must be reusable, accessible, responsive, typed, testable and explainable.

### Business Requirements
- Provide the core **Debounced search** behavior.
- Support normal, loading, empty and error states where applicable.
- Keep the public component API small and predictable.

### Functional Requirements
- User interactions must update UI state correctly.
- State must remain consistent after repeated interactions.
- Edge cases must not crash the application.
- Async work must handle cancellation/race conditions where applicable.

### Non-functional Requirements
- React 19+ and TypeScript
- Clean feature-based architecture
- Reusable components and hooks
- Responsive and accessible UI
- Testable behavior

### UI Requirements
- Use semantic HTML.
- Provide visible interaction states.
- Support mobile and desktop layouts.
- Provide loading, empty and error feedback when relevant.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Keyboard navigation must work.
- Interactive elements must have accessible names.
- Focus must be managed for overlays and composite widgets.
- ARIA must supplement—not replace—semantic HTML.

### Performance Requirements
- Avoid unnecessary rendering.
- Debounce/throttle high-frequency events where appropriate.
- Virtualize large lists/grids.
- Lazy-load expensive features.

### Responsive Requirements
Design mobile-first behavior, define layout breakpoints, preserve usable touch targets, and ensure content remains accessible at narrow widths.

### Problem Analysis
Identify the primary interaction model for **Debounced search**, then split it into presentational components, stateful logic, reusable hooks, data services and test boundaries.

### Low-Level Design
- Props define the public contract.
- Hooks own reusable behavior.
- Components render derived state.
- Services isolate API/network concerns.
- Utilities contain deterministic pure functions.

```text
 ↓
```

- Presentational primitives
- State/interaction hook

- Empty/loading/error components

### State Management Design
Keep ephemeral UI state local. Use Zustand/Redux Toolkit only when state is shared across independent consumers. Use TanStack Query for server state instead of duplicating request lifecycle state in global stores.

### API Layer Design
Expose typed service functions, centralize request behavior, normalize errors, support cancellation and keep credentials/security policy out of UI components.

### Custom Hooks

### Utilities
- Keep pure transformations in utilities.
- Unit test utilities independently.
- Avoid utilities that hide stateful behavior.

### Type Definitions
```ts

  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
};

};
```

### Constants
```ts
export const UI_LIMITS = {
  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Error Handling Strategy
Use typed application errors at the service boundary, local recoverable UI states for expected failures, and Error Boundaries for unexpected render failures.

### Loading Strategy
Prefer skeletons for stable layouts, spinners for short blocking operations, and Suspense/lazy loading for route or component boundaries.

### Empty State
Explain what is empty, why it is empty when known, and provide the most useful next action.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";

export function SearchBox() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");

  useEffect(() => {
    if (!query.trim()) return;
    const id = window.setTimeout(() => {
      console.log("search:", query);
    }, 300);
    return () => window.clearTimeout(id);
  }, [query]);

  return (
    <label>
      Search
      <input
        value={query}
        onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)}
        aria-label="Search"
      />
    </label>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

## Question 84 — Async suggestions

**Module:** Module 5 – Autocomplete & Search  
**Difficulty:** ⭐ Easy  
**Expected Time:** 20 Minutes  
**Experience Level:** 2–5 Years  
**Frequently Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Atlassian • Stripe • Uber • Airbnb

### Problem Statement
Build a production-quality **Async suggestions** component suitable for a machine-coding interview. The implementation must be reusable, accessible, responsive, typed, testable and explainable.

### Business Requirements
- Provide the core **Async suggestions** behavior.
- Support normal, loading, empty and error states where applicable.
- Keep the public component API small and predictable.

### Functional Requirements
- User interactions must update UI state correctly.
- State must remain consistent after repeated interactions.
- Edge cases must not crash the application.
- Async work must handle cancellation/race conditions where applicable.

### Non-functional Requirements
- React 19+ and TypeScript
- Clean feature-based architecture
- Reusable components and hooks
- Responsive and accessible UI
- Testable behavior

### UI Requirements
- Use semantic HTML.
- Provide visible interaction states.
- Support mobile and desktop layouts.
- Provide loading, empty and error feedback when relevant.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Keyboard navigation must work.
- Interactive elements must have accessible names.
- Focus must be managed for overlays and composite widgets.
- ARIA must supplement—not replace—semantic HTML.

### Performance Requirements
- Avoid unnecessary rendering.
- Debounce/throttle high-frequency events where appropriate.
- Virtualize large lists/grids.
- Lazy-load expensive features.

### Responsive Requirements
Design mobile-first behavior, define layout breakpoints, preserve usable touch targets, and ensure content remains accessible at narrow widths.

### Problem Analysis
Identify the primary interaction model for **Async suggestions**, then split it into presentational components, stateful logic, reusable hooks, data services and test boundaries.

### Low-Level Design
- Props define the public contract.
- Hooks own reusable behavior.
- Components render derived state.
- Services isolate API/network concerns.
- Utilities contain deterministic pure functions.

### High-Level Design
```text
Page
 ↓
Feature Container
 ├── UI Components
 ├── Custom Hooks
 ├── Query / API Layer
 ├── Client State
 └── Tests / Storybook
```

### Folder Structure
```text
src/
├── app/
├── components/
│   └── async-suggestions/
│       ├── async-suggestions.tsx
│       ├── async-suggestions.test.tsx
│       └── async-suggestions.stories.tsx
├── features/
├── hooks/
├── services/
├── store/
├── pages/
├── routes/
├── utils/
├── constants/
├── types/
├── styles/
└── tests/
```

### Project Architecture
Use feature-based boundaries so the component can evolve without creating a large shared-components dependency graph.

### Component Breakdown
- `Asyncsuggestions` container
- Presentational primitives
- State/interaction hook
- Async/data boundary if required
- Empty/loading/error components

### State Management Design
Keep ephemeral UI state local. Use Zustand/Redux Toolkit only when state is shared across independent consumers. Use TanStack Query for server state instead of duplicating request lifecycle state in global stores.

### API Layer Design
Expose typed service functions, centralize request behavior, normalize errors, support cancellation and keep credentials/security policy out of UI components.

### Custom Hooks
Suggested hook: `useAsyncSuggestions`. The hook should expose behavior, not DOM implementation details.

### Utilities
- Keep pure transformations in utilities.
- Unit test utilities independently.
- Avoid utilities that hide stateful behavior.

### Type Definitions
```ts
export type ComponentItem = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
  disabled?: boolean;
};

export type ComponentProps = {
  items: readonly ComponentItem[];
  onChange?: (item: ComponentItem) => void;
};
```

### Constants
```ts
export const UI_LIMITS = {
  debounceMs: 300,
  animationMs: 200,
  pageSize: 25,
} as const;
```

### Routing Strategy
Route-level features should be lazy-loaded where useful. URL state should be used for shareable filters, tabs, searches and navigation state.

### Error Handling Strategy
Use typed application errors at the service boundary, local recoverable UI states for expected failures, and Error Boundaries for unexpected render failures.

### Loading Strategy
Prefer skeletons for stable layouts, spinners for short blocking operations, and Suspense/lazy loading for route or component boundaries.

### Empty State
Explain what is empty, why it is empty when known, and provide the most useful next action.

### Edge Cases
- Empty input/data
- Duplicate items
- Slow network
- Failed requests
- Rapid repeated interaction
- Keyboard-only use
- Small viewport
- Very large data sets

### Scalability Considerations
Separate reusable UI primitives from feature-specific behavior. Normalize complex state, paginate server data, virtualize large collections and avoid global state for local concerns.

### Starter Implementation
```tsx
import { useState } from "react";

type Props = { items: string[] };

export function Component({ items }: Props) {
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string | null>(null);

  return (
    <section aria-label="Interactive component">
      {items.map((item) => (
        <button
          key={item}
          type="button"
          aria-pressed={selected === item}
          onClick={() => setSelected(item)}
        >
          {item}
        </button>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx
// Production pattern: isolate state, keep rendering pure,
// and expose a small typed API to consumers.
export type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

### Bad Implementation → Good Implementation
❌ **Bad:** put every state value in a global store, fetch directly from presentational components, duplicate interaction logic, omit keyboard support, and render thousands of nodes without virtualization.  
↓  
✅ **Good:** keep state local where possible, isolate server state in a query layer, extract reusable hooks, use semantic interaction patterns and measure/virtualize large collections.

### Expected Behavior
The **Async suggestions** component should remain predictable under normal use, repeated interactions, loading/error conditions and responsive layouts.

```text
User Event
   ↓
Handler
   ↓
State / Mutation
   ↓
Derived State
   ↓
Render
   ↓
Browser Paint
```

```text
Idle
 ├──→ Loading ──→ Success
 │                  └──→ Empty
 └──→ Error ──→ Retry
```

```text

   ↓
Custom Hook
   ↓
Query / Mutation Layer
   ↓
API Client
   ↓
Backend
```

### Performance Diagram
```text
Input
 ↓
Debounce / Batch
 ↓
Minimal State Update
 ↓
Selective Render
 ↓
Commit
 ↓
Paint
```

### Testing Strategy
- **Vitest:** pure utilities and hooks.
- **React Testing Library:** user-visible component behavior.
- **Playwright:** critical end-to-end flows.
- **Storybook:** isolated component states.
- **Accessibility:** keyboard and accessible-name assertions.

### Storybook Integration
```tsx
export const Default = {
  args: {
    items: [
      { id: "1", label: "First" },
      { id: "2", label: "Second" },
    ],
  },
};
```

### Deployment Considerations
- Production build with Vite.
- Environment-specific API configuration.
- Bundle analysis.
- Source-map policy appropriate to security requirements.
- CI checks for type errors, lint, unit tests and E2E smoke tests.

### Production Notes
Add observability for failures and latency, avoid logging sensitive data, verify responsive behavior, test slow networks and ensure accessibility regressions are caught before deployment.

### Accessibility Audit
- [ ] Semantic HTML
- [ ] Keyboard complete
- [ ] Focus visible
- [ ] Accessible names
- [ ] Error messages associated with controls
- [ ] Dynamic updates announced where required

### Performance Audit
- [ ] React DevTools Profiler reviewed
- [ ] No unnecessary global state
- [ ] Large collections virtualized
- [ ] Network requests debounced/cancelled where needed
- [ ] Lazy loading applied to appropriate boundaries
- [ ] Bundle impact measured

### Security Review
- [ ] Untrusted HTML is never rendered without a deliberate sanitization policy
- [ ] External URLs are validated
- [ ] Sensitive data is not placed in logs
- [ ] API authorization is enforced server-side
- [ ] Third-party dependencies are reviewed

### Interview Follow-up Questions
1. How would you make this component reusable across products?
2. How would you test keyboard and screen-reader behavior?
3. What happens with 100,000 records?
4. How would you handle slow or failed APIs?
5. Which state belongs locally versus globally?
6. Where would you use memoization, and how would you prove it helps?
7. How would you evolve the API without breaking consumers?
8. How would you instrument this in production?

### Time Complexity
For a typical list interaction, rendering is **O(n)** in the number of rendered items. With virtualization, the DOM work becomes approximately **O(v)** where `v` is the visible window, while data operations may remain O(n) depending on the algorithm.

### Space Complexity
Typical component state is **O(1)** or **O(n)** depending on whether selection/order/cache state is retained per item. Virtualization reduces DOM memory, not necessarily application data memory.

### Scalability Discussion
At Staff/Principal level, discuss component contracts, design-system governance, shared ownership, performance budgets, observability, versioning, accessibility compliance and migration strategy.

### Debugging Walkthrough
1. Reproduce the issue.
2. Inspect component props/state in React DevTools.
3. Profile renders with React Profiler.
4. Inspect network requests.
5. Check browser console and accessibility tree.
6. Add a focused regression test.
7. Re-measure after the fix.

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] Requirements are explicit
- [ ] Component API is minimal
- [ ] State ownership is justified
- [ ] Async race conditions handled
- [ ] Accessibility verified
- [ ] Responsive behavior verified
- [ ] Performance measured
- [ ] Tests cover behavior
- [ ] Storybook states exist
- [ ] Error/loading/empty states exist

### Mini Project
Build a complete **Async suggestions** feature with mock API support, loading/error/empty states, responsive design, accessibility audit, Storybook stories, Vitest tests and Playwright coverage.

### Production Exercise
Take the initial **Async suggestions** implementation and evolve it for enterprise scale: add server integration, caching, error recovery, telemetry, feature flags and performance instrumentation.

### Assignment
Implement **Async suggestions** in 45–60 minutes, then spend 15 minutes explaining architecture, trade-offs, accessibility, performance and testing decisions.

### Revision Notes
- Analyze → design → implement core path → handle states → accessibility → performance → testing → explain trade-offs.
- Prefer simple local state before introducing global state.
- Build reusable APIs, not reusable complexity.

### Cheat Sheet
**Requirements → LLD → HLD → Components → State → Hooks → API → Edge Cases → Accessibility → Performance → Tests → Storybook → Production.**

```tsx
  return (
    <section aria-label="Interactive component">
      {items.map((item) => (
        <button
          key={item}
          type="button"
          aria-pressed={selected === item}
          onClick={() => setSelected(item)}
        >
          {item}
        </button>
      ))}
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Alternative / Reusable Implementation
```tsx

// and expose a small typed API to consumers.

  id: string;
  label: string;
};

export function ItemList({
  items,
  onSelect,
}: {
  items: readonly Item[];
  onSelect: (item: Item) => void;
}) {
  return (
    <ul>
      {items.map((item) => (
        <li key={item.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(item)}>
            {item.label}
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

❌ **Bad:** put every state value in a global store, fetch directly from presentational components, duplicate interaction logic, omit keyboard support, and render thousands of nodes without virtualization.

```tsx
}
```
